To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the majority of colleges and universities do not require the SAT for admission to undergraduate programs; and (2) the majority of the institutions that do not require the test do not use it for admission purposes, either by themselves, or in combination with other measures, or in combination in the context of an optional policy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: Do institutions that have adopted a policy of not requiring the SAT for admission have more competitive admissions practices than institutions that require submission of SAT scores?
the impact of SAT/ACT requirements on the composition of the student body.
the effects on the college admissions process when a school makes the SAT optional.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence indicates that the SAT is not used as a significant factor in admissions at most colleges.
there is no evidence to support the claim that SATs are used in a discriminatory fashion.
the evidence does not permit us to conclude that the SAT has any substantial influence on the racial distribution of students in higher education.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is no single best way to measure academic aptitude, but that a combination of tests is better than a single test.
the SAT I and SAT II are not the only tests used to assess the potential of college students, but they are the most widely used tests in the nation.
we found that the SAT was not a significant factor in admissions, and that the use of the SAT was declining.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the SAT is not a good predictor of college performance.
the SAT is not a good indicator of college readiness.
the admissions process is complex and that there is no simple solution to the problem of how to make admissions decisions.
